title: The song of bliss
hook: tradition links his great hymn, the Anand Sahib, to joy at a grandson's birth; it is sung at every ceremony

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manji, a rope cot that became a teaching seat. Your line was she is not lesser. Whose voice did you make sure was heard? Day fifty-three.

Good news has a way of tumbling out before the hello is over. Mom, guess what. Guru Amar Das was an old man by now. Tradition says that a grandson was born to his son, Mohri, and the family was full of joy. The baby was named Anand. And around that time, tradition says, the Guru composed a hymn Sikhs still sing at every turn of life. It opens, in effect, with that same rush of good news, told to a mother. Today, the song.
screen: `GOOD NEWS, TUMBLING OUT.` → `MOM, GUESS WHAT.` → `A GRANDSON, AND A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Anand means bliss, deep joy, the kind that settles in rather than flashing past. The hymn has forty stanzas, in raga Ramkali, and its very first line goes something like this, in paraphrase: I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found my true Guru. Notice who the singer turns to with the news: mother, the one who has known the singer longest. And what's the news? Not wealth, not success. The singer has found the true Guru, and with that, the mind is at peace. The hymn goes on to say that this bliss can't be bought or faked, that it comes through the Guru's word, and it sings of the Word ringing inside like music. Tradition links the hymn to the grandson's birth, and the child and the hymn share a name. Here's why you may have heard it without knowing. The Anand Sahib, or its opening stanzas and last stanza, is sung at Sikh ceremonies of every kind. At a wedding. At a baby's naming. At the end of the congregation's prayers. Even at a funeral. Joy, on this path, isn't only for happy days; it's the steady bliss of being close to the Guru, which holds even when life is sad. Those same stanzas are part of Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer. A song that began with a family's joy now closes Sikh gatherings.
screen: `ANAND — DEEP, SETTLED JOY.` · `I AM IN BLISS, O MY MOTHER.` · `THE NEWS: I'VE FOUND THE TRUE GURU.` · `SUNG AT WEDDINGS, NAMINGS, FUNERALS.` · then, large: `BLISS, MOTHER, BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or hum something joyful. Nobody's listening, and it doesn't have to be good. Pick a tune that makes you glad: a lullaby, a hymn from your childhood, a song from a wedding you loved. Hum it softly, or sing it under your breath. Let your chest buzz with it. If a feeling of gladness comes, let it stay a moment. If it doesn't, that's fine; just keep the tune going. The bell holds the time.
Anand. Bliss, deep joy; the name of Guru Amar Das's grandson, and of the hymn that closes Sikh ceremonies. Today's word.
Your line: bliss, mother, bliss. Today, call or message someone who's known you a long time, and share one piece of good news. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: The Anand Sahib is part of the Sikh daily prayers, and its first five stanzas with the fortieth are sung at the close of congregational worship and at weddings, namings and funerals.

original.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; the Anand Sahib, and the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, share the word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a happy song.
what it means: settled bliss that comes from finding the true Guru, sung at joyful and sad occasions alike.
what a scholar hears: forty stanzas in Ramkali, from Ang 917; tradition links it to the birth of Anand, son of Mohri; six stanzas are sung to close congregational worship.
